title: Inter-Agent Relative Representations for Multi-Agent Option Discovery
claim: A joint state is factorised, compared against a team-aligned reference state, and aggregated into a representation from which coordination-capturing structure is learned.
layout: 1 panel, left-to-right, parallel branches merging at a sum, 3D surface output
description: A single left-to-right dataflow diagram. On the far left, a stacked bar labelled s_t (Joint state) splits into two branches. The top branch goes through a peach box g, which factorises the state into per-agent components s_t^0, s_t^1, ..., s_t^N. The bottom branch goes through a green trapezoid φ, which produces φ(s_t), the Fermat state, drawn in teal arrows. Each agent component and the Fermat state feed into a stack of blue trapezoids d_θ, the state distance encoders. Their outputs go into a peach Σ box. This gives a small bar labelled d_{F,t}, the n-distance. An orange trapezoid μ takes that bar and outputs a colourful 3D surface plot, which is the eigenvector. Braces and italic labels sit under the stages. Colour-coded boxes guide the eye along the flow.
caption: Option discovery on inter-agent relative representations for a state factorisation function $g$, Fermat encoder $\phi$, state distance encoder $d_\theta$ and a graph Laplacian eigenvector approximator $\mu$.
abstract: Temporally extended actions improve the ability to explore and plan in single-agent settings. In multi-agent settings, the exponential growth of the joint state space with the number of agents makes coordinated behaviours even more valuable. Yet, this same exponential growth renders the design of multi-agent options particularly challenging. Existing multi-agent option discovery methods often sacrifice coordination by producing loosely coupled or fully independent behaviours. Toward addressing these limitations, we describe a novel approach for multi-agent option discovery. Specifically, we propose a joint-state abstraction that compresses the state space while preserving the information necessary to discover strongly coordinated behaviours. Our approach builds on the inductive bias that synchronisation over agent states provides a natural foundation for coordination in the absence of explicit objectives. We first approximate a fictitious state of maximal alignment with the team, the \textit{Fermat} state, and use it to define a measure of \textit{spreadness}, capturing team-level misalignment on each individual state dimension. Building on this representation, we then employ a neural graph Laplacian estimator to derive options that capture state synchronisation patterns between agents. We evaluate the resulting options across multiple scenarios in two simulated multi-agent domains, showing that they yield stronger downstream coordination capabilities compared to alternative option discovery methods.
